questions.question: What are the three primary architectural tiers in modern web applications?

options.A: Client tier (Browser), Business Logic / Application tier (Server), Data tier (Database)
options.B: HTML tier, CSS tier, Font tier
options.C: Input tier, Processing tier, Output tier
options.D: Git tier, Docker tier, Cloud tier

questions.explanation: Web applications are organized as multi-tier architectures: Presentation/Client tier (browser/DOM), Business Logic tier (application server/APIs), and Data persistence tier (database).

questions.question: Why is client-side form validation alone (using JavaScript or HTML attributes) INSUFFICIENT for web application security and reliability?

options.A: Because client-side validation can be easily bypassed by attackers using tools like curl, Postman, or disabling JavaScript in the browser.
options.B: Because browsers do not support validation.
options.C: Because client-side validation slows down internet connections.
options.D: Because client-side validation only works on Windows.

questions.explanation: Never trust the client. Any malicious user can bypass browser validation by crafting raw HTTP requests directly to backend endpoints. Server-side validation is strictly mandatory.

questions.question: Because HTTP is fundamentally a stateless protocol, how do web applications maintain user session state across multiple requests?

options.A: Using Session Cookies, Server-side Sessions, URL rewriting, or LocalStorage / Token headers (e.g. JWT).
options.B: By keeping the TCP connection open forever.
options.C: By forcing users to re-login on every click.

questions.explanation: HTTP is stateless: each request is independent. Session tracking mechanisms (cookies containing session tokens, authorization headers, URL rewriting) tie requests to a persistent session.

questions.question: What is a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in web testing?

options.A: An injection attack where malicious client-side JavaScript scripts are injected into web pages viewed by other unsuspecting users.
options.B: When CSS stylesheets do not load.
options.C: When a link points to the wrong URL.

questions.explanation: XSS occurs when an application includes untrusted user input without proper HTML sanitization/escaping, allowing attacker scripts to run in victims' browsers and steal session cookies.

questions.question: What is SQL Injection (SQLi) and how is it tested?

options.A: Inserting malicious SQL query fragments into input fields to manipulate backend database queries; tested using payload strings like '' OR '1'='1'.
options.B: Injecting CSS into a web page.
options.C: Testing if SQL server runs on Linux.

questions.explanation: SQLi occurs when user input is concatenated directly into SQL statements without parameterized queries or ORM sanitization, allowing attackers to access or destroy data.

questions.question: What is Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)?

options.A: An attack that tricks an authenticated user's browser into transmitting unauthorized commands to a web application where the user is currently authenticated.
options.B: A broken hyperlink.

questions.explanation: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic inclusion of credentials (cookies) to execute unwanted actions on behalf of the victim; tested by checking for anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.

questions.question: What is 'Cross-Browser Compatibility Testing'?

options.A: Verifying that a web application renders correctly and functions identically across diverse web browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) and rendering engines.
options.B: Testing if two browsers can run at the same time.
options.D: Testing with all browser extensions enabled.

questions.explanation: Different browsers and layout engines (Blink, Gecko, WebKit) may interpret CSS rules, JavaScript features, and HTML elements differently, requiring compatibility verification.

questions.question: What is the Document Object Model (DOM) in web testing?

options.A: The in-memory hierarchical tree representation of the HTML document structure manipulated by client-side JavaScript.
options.B: A database format.

questions.explanation: The DOM represents the page structure as a tree of objects. Functional testing frameworks (e.g. Selenium, Playwright, Cypress) interact directly with DOM nodes.

questions.question: Why is testing Asynchronous JavaScript and XML (AJAX) / Fetch requests more complex than traditional static page testing?

options.A: Because updates occur dynamically and asynchronously in the background without a full page reload, introducing timing dependencies and race conditions for test assertions.
options.B: Because AJAX requests do not use HTTP.
options.C: Because AJAX only works in Chrome.

questions.explanation: Asynchronous calls mean elements appear or change state dynamically over time; test scripts must use explicit waits rather than hardcoded sleeps to avoid synchronization flakiness.

questions.question: What is 'Broken Link Testing' on static web sites?

options.A: Crawling all hyperlinks (anchor tags) to verify that none return HTTP 404 (Not Found) or 500 (Server Error) status codes.
options.B: Checking if the keyboard works.

questions.explanation: Hyperlink verification spiders through site URLs to ensure that internal navigation anchors, assets (images, stylesheets), and external links resolve successfully.

questions.question: In web testing, what does an HTTP 500 status code indicate?

options.A: Internal Server Error: an unhandled exception occurred on the backend server.
options.B: The page was found successfully.

questions.explanation: HTTP 500 indicates an unexpected condition on the server that prevented it from fulfilling the request, signaling a server-side bug or crash.

questions.question: What is 'Responsive Web Design (RWD) Testing'?

options.A: Testing that the layout, fonts, and controls dynamically adapt gracefully across different viewport widths and screen resolutions (mobile, tablet, desktop).
options.B: Testing how fast the server responds.

questions.explanation: RWD testing checks CSS media queries and fluid grids to ensure visual elements remain legible, interactive, and free from horizontal scrolling across various device widths.

questions.question: What is the 'Page Object Model' (POM) design pattern in automated web testing?

options.A: A pattern that encapsulates web page elements and interactions into dedicated class objects, separating test logic from DOM selector details.
options.B: A pattern that converts web pages into PDF documents.
options.C: A database schema for web pages.
options.D: A tool that writes HTML code.

questions.explanation: POM enhances test maintenance by modeling pages as classes with methods representing services offered by the page, insulating test cases from changes in HTML markup and selectors.

questions.question: What is the purpose of testing browser LocalStorage and SessionStorage?

options.A: To verify that client-persisted state, preferences, and offline tokens are accurately saved, retrieved, and cleared upon logout.
options.B: To measure hard drive spin rates.

questions.explanation: Web Storage APIs store key-value data on the client. Testing ensures data integrity, quota handling, and that sensitive authentication artifacts are invalidated on logout.

questions.question: What is 'Session Hijacking' and how is it mitigated and tested?

options.A: An attacker steals a valid session ID to impersonate the user; tested by verifying the use of HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags and HTTPS encryption.
options.B: When a user logs out.

questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies prevent JavaScript from accessing session tokens (mitigating XSS theft), and Secure flags ensure cookies are only transmitted over TLS/HTTPS.

questions.question: What is Web Accessibility Testing (WCAG compliance)?

options.A: Evaluating whether a web application is usable by individuals with disabilities, including screen reader support, keyboard navigation, and color contrast.
options.B: Testing if the website is available 24/7.

questions.explanation: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) outlines standards for perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust content, verified via accessibility audits and screen readers.

questions.question: In REST API testing for web backends, what are the standard expectations for idempotency of HTTP methods?

options.A: GET, PUT, and DELETE should be idempotent (multiple identical requests have the same side-effect as one); POST is typically non-idempotent.
options.B: All HTTP methods must be non-idempotent.
options.D: Idempotency only applies to email servers.

questions.explanation: Idempotent HTTP methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) guarantee that repeating the request multiple times produces the exact same server state as a single invocation.

questions.question: What is 'DOM XSS' (Document Object Model-based Cross-Site Scripting)?

options.A: An XSS vulnerability that executes entirely on the client side when unsafe JavaScript sinks (like innerHTML or eval) consume data from untrusted sources (like location.search).
options.B: An error in the database server.

questions.explanation: In DOM XSS, the malicious payload never touches the backend server; client-side JavaScript reads from an untrusted source (document.location) and writes directly to an unsafe sink (element.innerHTML).

questions.question: What is a 'Content Security Policy' (CSP) header in web security?

options.A: An HTTP header that restricts the domains and resource types (scripts, images, styles) that the browser is permitted to load and execute.
options.B: A copyright statement on the homepage.

questions.explanation: CSP is a powerful defense-in-depth header that mitigates XSS and data injection by whitelisting trusted script origins and disabling unauthorized inline scripts.

questions.question: What is headless browser testing?

options.A: Running automated browser tests without rendering a graphical user interface (GUI) on screen, enabling fast execution in CI/CD environments.
options.B: Testing without a keyboard.
options.D: Testing code that has no main method.

questions.explanation: Headless browsers (e.g. headless Chrome, Puppeteer, Playwright) execute the real browser engine in memory without UI rendering overhead, ideal for automated pipelines.
